## <span class="num">13.5.1</span> Invariants and the Inner Product on Class Functions

:::proposition{13.5.1} Averaging projection
Let $V$ be a representation of $G$, and let $$\varphi_V = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} g : V \to V.$$ Then $\varphi_V$ is a projection onto $V^G$: its image is $V^G$, and it is the identity on $V^G$. Consequently, $$\dim V^G = \Tr(\varphi_V) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\chi_V(g).$$
:::

:::proof
If $v \in V^G$, every term $gv$ equals $v$, so $\varphi_V(v) = v$. For any $v \in V$ and $h \in G$, $$h\,\varphi_V(v) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} hgv = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g' \in G} g'v = \varphi_V(v),$$ since $g' = hg$ runs over $G$ as $g$ does; so $\varphi_V(v) \in V^G$. Thus $\Img\varphi_V = V^G$ and $\varphi_V^2 = \varphi_V$. Then $V = \Img\varphi_V \oplus \ker\varphi_V$: every $v$ is $\varphi_V(v) + (v - \varphi_V(v))$ with $v - \varphi_V(v) \in \ker\varphi_V$, and a vector $v$ in both summands satisfies $v = \varphi_V(v) = 0$. In a basis adapted to this decomposition, $\varphi_V$ has matrix $\diag(1, \ldots, 1, 0, \ldots, 0)$ with $\dim V^G$ ones, so $\Tr\varphi_V = \dim V^G$. By linearity of the trace, $\Tr\varphi_V = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g\Tr\rho(g) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g\chi_V(g)$.
:::

:::corollary{13.5.2} Dimension of $\Hom_G$
For representations $V$ and $W$ of $G$, $$\dim\Hom_G(V, W) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\ol{\chi_V(g)}\,\chi_W(g).$$
:::

:::proof
By Proposition [13.1.10](/notes/math-55a/13-1-representations-and-subrepresentations#proposition-13-1-10), $\Hom_G(V, W) = \Hom(V, W)^G$. Apply Proposition [13.5.1](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#proposition-13-5-1) to the representation $\Hom(V, W)$, and use $\chi_{\Hom(V, W)} = \ol{\chi_V}\,\chi_W$ (Proposition [13.4.3](/notes/math-55a/13-4-characters#proposition-13-4-3)).
:::

This formula suggests an inner product. Let $\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$ denote the complex vector space of class functions on $G$. A class function is determined by its values on the conjugacy classes, and these values can be chosen freely, so the indicator functions of the conjugacy classes form a basis of $\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$. In particular, $\dim\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$ is the number of conjugacy classes of $G$.

:::definition{13.5.3} Inner product on class functions
For class functions $\alpha$ and $\beta$ on $G$, let $$H(\alpha, \beta) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\ol{\alpha(g)}\,\beta(g).$$
:::

This $H$ is a positive-definite Hermitian inner product on $\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$. It is conjugate-linear in the first variable and linear in the second, the convention of Chapter 9; it satisfies $H(\beta, \alpha) = \ol{H(\alpha, \beta)}$; and $H(\alpha, \alpha) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g|\alpha(g)|^2 > 0$ for $\alpha \neq 0$. Grouping the terms by conjugacy classes, $$H(\alpha, \beta) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{C}|C|\,\ol{\alpha(C)}\,\beta(C),$$ where $C$ runs over the conjugacy classes of $G$ and $\alpha(C)$ denotes the value of $\alpha$ on $C$. This is the form in which we compute with character tables.

:::theorem{13.5.4} Orthogonality of characters
For representations $V$ and $W$ of $G$, $H(\chi_V, \chi_W) = \dim\Hom_G(V, W)$. In particular, if $V$ and $W$ are irreducible, then $$H(\chi_V, \chi_W) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V \cong W, \\ 0 & \text{if } V \not\cong W. \end{cases}$$ So the characters of pairwise non-isomorphic irreducible representations are orthonormal with respect to $H$.
:::

:::proof
The first statement is Corollary [13.5.2](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#corollary-13-5-2), and the second follows from it by Corollary [13.3.2](/notes/math-55a/13-3-schurs-lemma#corollary-13-3-2).
:::

:::corollary{13.5.5} At most as many irreducibles as conjugacy classes
Up to isomorphism, $G$ has finitely many irreducible representations, and their number is at most the number of conjugacy classes of $G$.
:::

:::proof
Orthonormal vectors are linearly independent: if $\sum_i c_i\chi_{V_i} = 0$, applying $H(\chi_{V_j}, -)$ gives $c_j = 0$. So the characters of pairwise non-isomorphic irreducible representations form a linearly independent subset of $\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$, and there are at most $\dim\CC_{\mathrm{class}}(G)$ of them.
:::

From now on, $V_1, \ldots, V_k$ denote the irreducible representations of $G$, one from each isomorphism class, with characters $\chi_i = \chi_{V_i}$ and dimensions $n_i = \dim V_i$. So far we know that $k$ is at most the number of conjugacy classes; Theorem [13.6.2](/notes/math-55a/13-6-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis#theorem-13-6-2) below shows that the two numbers are equal.

:::corollary{13.5.6} A representation is determined by its character
Let $W$ be a representation of $G$. In any decomposition of $W$ into irreducible subrepresentations, the number of summands isomorphic to $V_i$ is $$a_i = H(\chi_i, \chi_W) = \dim\Hom_G(V_i, W).$$ So $W \cong \bigoplus_i V_i^{\oplus a_i}$, and the multiplicities $a_i$ do not depend on the decomposition. Two representations with the same character are isomorphic.
:::

:::proof
If $W \cong \bigoplus_i V_i^{\oplus a_i}$ (Corollary [13.2.3](/notes/math-55a/13-2-maschkes-theorem-and-complete-reducibility#corollary-13-2-3)), then $\chi_W = \sum_i a_i\chi_i$ by Proposition [13.4.3](/notes/math-55a/13-4-characters#proposition-13-4-3), and $H(\chi_j, \chi_W) = \sum_i a_iH(\chi_j, \chi_i) = a_j$ by Theorem [13.5.4](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#theorem-13-5-4). So the $a_i$ are determined by $\chi_W$, and two representations with the same character have the same multiplicities, hence are isomorphic.
:::

:::corollary{13.5.7} Irreducibility criterion
If $W \cong \bigoplus_i V_i^{\oplus a_i}$, then $H(\chi_W, \chi_W) = \sum_i a_i^2$. In particular, $W$ is irreducible if and only if $H(\chi_W, \chi_W) = 1$.
:::

:::proof
By orthonormality, $H(\chi_W, \chi_W) = \sum_{i,j}a_ia_jH(\chi_i, \chi_j) = \sum_i a_i^2$. This sum of squares of nonnegative integers equals $1$ exactly when one $a_i$ is $1$ and the others are $0$, that is, when $W \cong V_i$ for some $i$.
:::

:::note
The number $H(\chi_W, \chi_W)$ is a quick count of the irreducible pieces of $W$. For small values it says:

<div class="table-wrap"><table class="tex-table"><thead><tr><th scope="col" class="c">$H(\chi_W, \chi_W)$</th><th scope="col" class="c">$W$ is</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td class="c">$1$</td><td class="c">irreducible;</td></tr><tr><td class="c">$2$</td><td class="c">a direct sum of two non-isomorphic irreducibles;</td></tr><tr><td class="c">$3$</td><td class="c">a direct sum of three pairwise non-isomorphic irreducibles;</td></tr><tr><td class="c">$4$</td><td class="c">a direct sum of four pairwise non-isomorphic irreducibles, or $X \oplus X$ for an irreducible $X$.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
:::

Twisting by a $1$-dimensional representation is a cheap way to produce new irreducible representations from old ones.

:::proposition{13.5.8} Twisting by a $1$-dimensional representation
Let $L$ be a $1$-dimensional representation of $G$, given by a homomorphism $\theta : G \to \CC^*$. For every representation $V$ of $G$, $\chi_{V \otimes L} = \theta\,\chi_V$, and $V \otimes L$ is irreducible if and only if $V$ is.
:::

:::proof
Fix a basis vector $\ell$ of $L$. The map $\iota : V \to V \otimes L$, $v \mapsto v \otimes \ell$, is a linear isomorphism, and $$g\,\iota(v) = gv \otimes \theta(g)\ell = \iota\bigl(\theta(g)\,gv\bigr).$$ So, transported by $\iota$, $g$ acts on $V \otimes L$ as the operator $\theta(g)\rho(g)$ acts on $V$; taking traces gives $\chi_{V \otimes L} = \theta\,\chi_V$. A subspace of $V$ is invariant under all the operators $\theta(g)\rho(g)$ if and only if it is invariant under all $\rho(g)$, because the $\theta(g)$ are nonzero scalars. Hence $\iota$ matches the subrepresentations of $V$ with those of $V \otimes L$, and one is irreducible exactly when the other is.
:::

## <span class="num">13.5.2</span> The Regular Representation

:::definition{13.5.9} Regular representation
The ***regular representation*** $R$ of $G$ is the permutation representation for the action of $G$ on itself by left multiplication: $R = {\CC}[G]$ has basis $\{e_h\}_{h \in G}$, and $g\,e_h = e_{gh}$.
:::

:::proposition{13.5.10} Decomposition of the regular representation
Each irreducible representation $V_i$ occurs in $R$ with multiplicity $n_i = \dim V_i$: $R \cong \bigoplus_i V_i^{\oplus n_i}$.
:::

:::proof
By Proposition [13.4.3](/notes/math-55a/13-4-characters#proposition-13-4-3)(v), $\chi_R(g)$ is the number of $h \in G$ with $gh = h$, which is $|G|$ if $g = e$ and $0$ otherwise. By Corollary [13.5.6](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#corollary-13-5-6), the multiplicity of $V_i$ in $R$ is $$H(\chi_i, \chi_R) = \frac{1}{|G|}\,\ol{\chi_i(e)}\,|G| = \dim V_i.$$
:::

:::corollary{13.5.11} Sum of squares of the dimensions
$\sum_{i=1}^k n_i^2 = |G|$.
:::

:::proof
Compare dimensions in Proposition [13.5.10](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#proposition-13-5-10): $|G| = \dim R = \sum_i n_i\dim V_i = \sum_i n_i^2$.
:::
